hook: In 1941 Viktor Frankl held an American visa that would have saved his life, and a piece of stone his father had picked up from a burned synagogue. He let the visa expire. What he learned in the four camps that followed became the most quietly powerful book ever written about why people endure.

p: Frankl was a Viennese neurologist and psychiatrist, head of a hospital department, with a manuscript and a career ahead of him. The visa was for him alone. If he used it, his elderly parents stayed behind, and by 1941 nobody in Vienna had illusions about what that meant.

He came home undecided and found a fragment of marble on the table. His father had taken it from the ruins of a synagogue the National Socialists had burned. From the single Hebrew letter on it, he could identify which of the Ten Commandments it came from. Only one commandment began with that letter: honour thy father and thy mother.

He stayed. Over the next three years he was held in four camps. His father died at Theresienstadt, his mother at Auschwitz, his brother in the camps, and his pregnant wife Tilly at Bergen-Belsen. He wrote this book in nine days in 1946 and intended to publish it anonymously.

Frankl organises the camp experience as a psychiatrist, in three phases. First, shock on arrival: the officer at Auschwitz flicking one finger left or right, a gesture as casual as waving away a fly, that sent roughly nine in ten of his transport straight to the crematorium. Alongside the terror came black humour, and what he calls the delusion of reprieve, the condemned man's conviction that he will somehow be pardoned.

Second, apathy: a protective emotional death. Men who once felt sick at the sight of a beating watched with distant, procedural interest. Frankl notes clinically that the textbooks are wrong about what a human being can survive, and that chronic illnesses vanished under conditions no textbook would predict anyone could endure at all.

Third, and most surprising, liberation. Not joy but depersonalisation. Men walked out into meadows, saw flowers, and felt nothing. The capacity for joy had to be relearned like a wasted muscle, and for many the return home brought a worse blow: nobody was waiting.

sections.h: The Last Of The Human Freedoms
p: Frankl describes the few men who walked through the huts comforting others and giving away their last piece of bread. There were not many, he says, but they were enough. They offer sufficient proof that everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances. Note what he does not claim. Attitude did not save those men, and suffering is not good. He is making a narrower, harder claim: when every other option has been removed, one remains, and it decides who the person is at the end.

Then philosophy becomes clinical data. Frankl watched men lose their grip on the future and then die, physically, within days. The signal was recognisable: a prisoner would refuse to get up, then smoke the cigarettes that functioned as camp currency. Everyone knew he would be dead within about forty eight hours, and he was.

A fellow prisoner dreamed a voice told him the war would end for him on the thirtieth of March. As the date neared and liberation clearly was not coming, his hope collapsed. He fell ill with typhus on the twenty ninth, lost consciousness on the thirtieth, and died on the thirty first. The dream did not kill him. The loss of his future did. The same pattern appeared as a statistic: deaths rose sharply in the week between Christmas 1944 and the New Year, beyond anything the weather or the rations explained, because so many men had been living on the naive hope of being home by Christmas.
sections.pull: He who has a why to live can bear with almost any how.

p: Frankl's great reversal: it did not matter what we expected from life, but rather what life expected from us. Stop asking what you are getting. Every hour puts a question to you, and you answer it with what you actually do. He splits the word responsibility to show his meaning: response, and ability.

Two men told him separately that they intended to kill themselves, both using the identical phrase, that they had nothing more to expect from life. He turned it around and made it concrete. For one it was a child abroad who was waiting and who had no other father. For the other, an unfinished series of books nobody else could complete.

Meaning, he insists, is never general. There is no meaning of life in the abstract any more than there is a best move in chess in the abstract. There is only the right move for this position, for this player, now.

Meaning is detected, not invented, and it can be found in three ways. By creating a work or doing a deed. By experiencing something or encountering someone, above all through love. And by the attitude taken towards unavoidable suffering.

The case that makes it land: an elderly doctor, two years into a depression after his wife's death. Frankl asked one question. What would have happened if you had died first and she had survived you? The man said it would have been terrible, how she would have suffered. Frankl said: such suffering has been spared her, and it was you who spared her, but now you pay for it by surviving and mourning her.

Nothing was cured. The suffering did not shrink by a gram. But it now had a meaning, and Frankl's line is that suffering ceases to be suffering the moment it finds one. He fences this carefully: if the suffering is avoidable, remove the cause. Unnecessary suffering is masochism, not heroism.
sections.pull: When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.

p: Logotherapy's practical technique, still used today. Anticipatory anxiety produces exactly what it fears: the man afraid of blushing blushes, the man trying to sleep stays awake. Things like sleep and pleasure are by-products that vanish when pursued directly.

So invert the wish. A young doctor with a four year phobia about sweating was told that whenever it started he should resolve to show people just how much he could sweat, to pour out ten quarts instead of one. He was free of it inside a week. The humour creates distance, and the distance breaks the loop, because you cannot fear what you are actively trying to achieve.

The same principle governs his advice about ambition. Do not aim at success. The more you make it a target the more you will miss it. It must ensue as the side effect of dedication to something greater than yourself.

Frankl's answer to the tragic triad of pain, guilt and death is what he calls tragic optimism: turn suffering into achievement, take from guilt the chance to change, and let life's transitoriness push you to act responsibly now.

People look at time passing and see only the stubble field of what is gone. They fail to see the full granaries into which they have already brought the harvest: the deeds done, the loves lived, the sufferings borne well. Having been is the surest kind of being there is, and nothing that comes later can undo it.

He refused any notion of collective guilt, and said there are only two races of men, the decent and the indecent, and both are found in every group. He lived to ninety two, earned a pilot's licence at sixty seven, and disliked being told his message was that suffering is good. It is not. His message is that suffering happens, and its meaning is the one thing about it you can still decide.

takeaways: Reverse the question. When you catch yourself asking what you are getting from a job or a relationship, ask instead what is being asked of you here, right now.
Name what depends on you specifically, a person or a piece of work that nobody else can do the same way. That is the why that lets you bear almost any how.
If your suffering is avoidable, remove the cause. Frankl is emphatic on this and it is the part people skip.
When a situation genuinely cannot be changed, put your attention on what you can still choose about your response, as a way of keeping the one thing that cannot be taken.
For anticipatory anxiety, try paradoxical intention: aim, with as much humour as you can find, to produce the very thing you dread.
Stop chasing happiness or success directly. Pick a cause, a person or a work outside yourself and let both arrive as side effects.
Live as if you were living for the second time, and as if you had acted the first time as wrongly as you are about to act now.
